extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, advocates of free expression, and general readers interested in arguments for free discussion
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical argument for why free, open, and adversarial discussion is essential to know, preserve, and advance truth in moral, religious, political, and practical matters. Emphasises educational, social, and institutional practices that sustain meaningful belief and prevent doctrines from becoming dead dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free and frequent fearless discussion of received opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: “However true [an opinion] may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition and repeated public contestation keep beliefs alive and prevent them from becoming mere rote phrases. Absence of such discussion causes opinions to be received as prejudice rather than understood conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and be able to defend the grounds of one's opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the cultivation of the understanding consists in one thing more than in another, it is surely in learning the grounds of one's own opinions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On important subjects, individuals ought to understand reasons for their beliefs and be able to defend them at least against common objections; merely parroting doctrines is inadequate intellectual cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance conflicting reasons; truth depends on confronting opposing arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: “On every subject on which difference of opinion is possible, the truth depends on a balance to be struck between two sets of conflicting reasons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike mathematics, most human subjects have plausible objections and rival explanations; arriving at truth requires confronting and weighing opposing accounts, not accepting a single-sided exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hear opposing arguments in their strongest, earnest form
rubrics_metrics.description: “He must be able to hear them from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest, and do their very utmost for them. He must know them in their most plausible and persuasive form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To truly understand and be able to refute (or accommodate) an opposing view, one must engage with the opponent’s best case, not a weakened or caricatured version presented by one’s own side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of judgment is rational when one lacks acquaintance with opposing reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that... The rational position for him would be suspension of judgment.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one cannot answer the strongest reasons on the other side (or does not even know them), preferring one opinion over another is irrational; the appropriate stance is to suspend judgment until both sides are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching must not present adversary views only to refute them; direct engagement is needed
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not enough that he should hear the arguments of adversaries from his own teachers, presented as they state them, and accompanied by what they offer as refutations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing an opponent’s position only as framed and answered by one’s teachers fails to give the learner a real grasp of the opposing case; learners should encounter opponents’ arguments as their champions present them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public access to objections is necessary even if specialists answer them
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mankind ought to have a rational assurance that all objections have been satisfactorily answered; and how are they to be answered if that which requires to be answered is not spoken?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if only experts can satisfactorily respond, objections must be openly stated so that answers can be tested; keeping objections hidden prevents assurance that they have been properly met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to write and publish without restraint for teachers and thinkers
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the teachers of mankind are to be cognisant of all that they ought to know, everything must be free to be written and published without restraint.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censorship that prevents dissemination of dissenting views undermines teachers’ ability to learn objections and hampers the intellectual obligations of those who must answer criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shutting out discussion produces parroted beliefs and intellectual stagnation
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a class of persons... who think it enough if a person assents undoubtingly... though he has no knowledge whatever of the grounds of the opinion... This is not knowing the truth. Truth, thus held, is but one superstition the more.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denying discussion leads to unexamined assent, where doctrines persist as untested prejudices; even if arguments get in later, beliefs held without understanding are fragile and unserious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion preserves the meaning and vitality of doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not only the grounds of the opinion are forgotten in the absence of discussion, but too often the meaning of the opinion itself... Instead of a vivid conception and a living belief, there remain only a few phrases retained by rote.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controversy keeps doctrines connected to their implications and lived effect; without it, the language of doctrine outlives its felt meaning and practical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative criticism (dialectic) is indispensable as a means to positive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: “Negative criticism—that which points out weaknesses in theory or errors in practice... as a means to attaining any positive knowledge or conviction worthy the name, it cannot be valued too highly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although negative logic is not an ultimate end, training in pointing out flaws and counterarguments is crucial for forming sound positive convictions; neglecting it lowers the general level of intellect outside mathematical and physical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissenting opinions often supply missing parts of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “When the conflicting doctrines, instead of being one true and the other false, share the truth between them; and the nonconforming opinion is needed to supply the remainder of the truth...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular opinions are often partial; minority or heretical views frequently contain neglected truths that should be considered and can correct one-sided mainstream views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both opposing political tendencies deserve expression and encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: “A party of order or stability, and a party of progress or reform, are both necessary elements of a healthy state of political life... Each of these modes of thinking derives its utility from the deficiencies of the other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical truth in politics often arises from reconciling opposites; the minority side frequently represents neglected interests and should be tolerated and encouraged to ensure balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat received principles as complete, unchallengeable truths
rubrics_metrics.description: “It may be objected, ‘But some received principles... are more than half-truths...’ Before pronouncing what Christian morality is or is not, it would be desirable to decide what is meant by Christian morality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully define terms and examine historical and contextual limits of accepted doctrines; many established moral or religious principles are partial, historically situated, and in need of supplementation or reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational practice should recreate adversarial discipline (Socratic dialectic)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Socratic dialectics... were essentially a negative discussion of the great questions... intended to make sure that the pupil understood his own opinion, and (by necessary correlation) the opinion opposed to it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical disputational practices trained minds to grasp both sides; modern education lacks adequate substitution and should seek contrivances that force learners to consider difficulties as if pressed by an opponent.
